- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift downward by 1–2%.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >75% of 30d mean), model often overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at +3–5% above peak or add a 1–2 day lag.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.8) and price is trending up, model may overfit upward momentum; apply mean reversion bias: subtract 0.5–1.5% from forecast if price > 78.
- When true outcome shows strong downward correction after a peak, model often fails to recognize it; add a 1–3 day “reversion buffer” to forecast.
- For 30d forecasts, if history shows volatility >10% over 5 days, model tends to smooth too much; allow 1–2% volatility buffer in forecast range.
- If sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 0.8, 0.0, 0.8), model may misinterpret sentiment cycles; adjust forecast to reflect sentiment “weight” — e.g., if sentiment drops, reduce forecast slope by 0.2–0.4 per day.
